model.name: Four-compartment test model
model.description: A four-compartment test model. C1 drains to C2 and C3, C2 feeds C3, and C3 discharges to C4. The Outflow expression is the discharge rate times C3, so the release curve can be read directly.

model.name: Neptunium series ingrowth
model.description: A single compartment holding pure Pu-241, showing ingrowth down the 4n+1 chain: Pu-241 to Am-241 to Np-237 to U-233 to Th-229. Nothing moves between compartments here; every feature on the chart comes from the decay and ingrowth terms. The inventories are activities, so a daughter grows in at its own decay constant: Am-241 lives 30 times longer than the Pu-241 feeding it and its activity peaks 34 times lower. Set decay_unit to mol to count atoms instead, and the same run conserves the chain down it.

model.name: Canisters failing: a source term with barriers, and two disruptive events
model.description: 4,500 spent-fuel canisters in a repository. None fails before year 1,000; after that the failures follow a Weibull with a characteristic life of 50,000 years and a shape of 2, the corrosion form. When a canister fails, 3% of its caesium and 0.5% of the rest is in the water at once (the instant release fraction) and the remainder waits for the fuel matrix, which dissolves at one part in ten million a year. The release goes into the near-field water, which is flushed to the geosphere; switch the mass-balance audit on under SIMULATION to watch the bookkeeping close. Two disruptive events act on it: an earthquake, a Poisson process at 2e-5 a year that fails 5% of the still-intact canisters at each occurrence, and a glaciation at 100,000 years that strips 80% of the biosphere out of the model. A deterministic run takes the earthquake in its expected-value form; a probabilistic run draws its occurrences — compare the staircase of Quake with its expected line.

parameters.name: t_first_failure
parameters.comment: No canister fails before this: the time the earliest corrosion process could breach one.

parameters.name: canister_life
parameters.comment: The Weibull scale: 63% of the canisters have failed one life after the first failure.

parameters.name: matrix_rate
parameters.comment: The fraction of the exposed fuel matrix dissolving per year. Everything bound in it leaves congruently.

parameters.name: flush_rate
parameters.comment: Turnover of the near-field water: the fraction leaving for the geosphere per year.

parameters.name: geo_rate
parameters.comment: Transit through the geosphere to the biosphere, as a first-order rate.

parameters.name: quake_rate
parameters.comment: Earthquakes breaching canisters: one in fifty thousand years.

parameters.name: t_glacial
parameters.comment: When the next ice sheet reaches the site.

waste_packages.name: Canisters
waste_packages.comment: The source term: the inventory starts inside the canisters and reaches the water only as they fail and the fuel dissolves. What leaves is the line drawn out of the block.

compartments.name: NearField
compartments.comment: The water in and around the failed canisters. A solubility limit would go on the transfer out of here, as an availability.

transfers.name: Release
transfers.comment: What leaves the canisters. Its rate is the block itself, so there is nothing to set.

transfers.name: Loss
transfers.comment: Dilution and dispersal out of the modelled biosphere.

events.name: Quake
events.comment: An earthquake: at each occurrence 5% of the canisters still intact fail. Deterministically a hazard of 1e-6 a year on the intact inventory; in a probabilistic run, drawn occurrences.

events.name: Glaciation
events.comment: The ice sheet arrives: 80% of what the biosphere holds is scraped away, out of the model.

model.name: Landscape objects, two dimensions
model.description: Four nuclides moving through three landscape objects. Compartments are indexed by Radionuclides x Object, so each box on the diagram is really 12 state variables. Sorption is per nuclide, discharge is per object, and the Wetland sub-set drains only the lake and the mire. The three reductions show the two ways of collapsing a dimension: Inventory adds two blocks index by index, TotalWater sums one block over the nuclides, and PeakObject takes the largest object for each nuclide. Solved with the NDF solver, which handles the stiffness from Pb-210 and Ra-226 in a fraction of the steps the Rosenbrock pair needs.

parameters.name: Kd
parameters.comment: Sorption: nuclide specific, shared across objects

parameters.name: discharge
parameters.comment: Water turnover: object specific, shared across nuclides

parameters.name: rho
parameters.comment: Bulk density of the solid, in the retardation factor.

parameters.name: porosity
parameters.comment: Water-filled porosity, in the retardation factor.

transfers.name: Discharge
transfers.comment: Every object discharges into the one downstream compartment, so this flux is summed over Object on the way in. That is what sum_extra_indices asks for; without it the model is refused, because a flux whose ends do not correspond is far more often a mistake than an intention.

transfers.name: WetlandLoss
transfers.comment: Only the wetlands lose water this way; the forest does not. Indexed by Radionuclides x Wetland, and the Wetland sub-set resolves onto the Object dimension of the compartments.

index_reductions.name: TotalWater
index_reductions.comment: Every nuclide in the water of each object -- the sum this used to spell out by hand.

index_reductions.name: PeakObject
index_reductions.comment: The worst object for each nuclide.

block_reductions.name: Inventory
block_reductions.comment: Regolith and water together, object by object.

model.name: Fractured rock: a far-field path
model.description:
A waste vault leaks into a fracture in the host rock; the nuclides travel along it by advection, sorb on the fracture coating and diffuse into the pore water of the rock matrix beside it, and what survives the journey reaches a well. The rock is one FARFCOMP block — a dual-porosity transport model ported from SKB's own farf_comp, with 20 fracture cells and 20 matrix layers per nuclide behind it, and the rock going on past the point the release is measured, as in FARF31 — and the whole thing is solved as one system with the two compartments.

The three nuclides are a decay chain, and they decay and grow into one another everywhere: in the vault, in every cell of the fracture, in every layer of the rock, and in the well. Th-230 hardly reaches the well as itself; almost all of what arrives grew in on the way.

Try: the travel time TW and the flow resistance F are what a hydrogeological model supplies, so change them and watch the arrival move. Turn on "Report every cell" in the block's Discretisation section to chart the profile down the fracture and into the rock.

parameters.name: leach_rate
parameters.comment: How fast the vault gives up its inventory to the fracture.

parameters.name: well_flow
parameters.comment: The volume the well draws, which dilutes what arrives.

parameters.name: well_volume
parameters.comment: The water in the well that what arrives mixes into. The flow over it is how often that water is replaced: a thousand times a year, so the well's inventory is a steady state.

parameters.name: Kd_matrix
parameters.comment: Sorption in the rock matrix, per nuclide. Thorium is held far harder than uranium, which is why it arrives so much later.

parameters.name: De_matrix
parameters.comment: Effective diffusivity: 1e-12 m2/s in the pore water.

compartments.name: Vault
compartments.comment: The waste. Only U-238 is emplaced; the other two grow in.

compartments.name: Well
compartments.comment: What arrives, before it is drawn off.

farfields.name: Rock
farfields.comment: SKB's FARFCOMP. TW is the water travel time along the path and F the flow-related transport resistance; the rest is the rock and the chemistry. The first matrix layer is left empty, so it is worked out from the path's own time scales — 3.6 mm here, growing by 1.44 to 12.5 m — and the rock goes on past the release point: five cells of it stand for the rock downstream, and what is in them has been released.

transfers.name: Leach
transfers.comment: Into the first cell of the fracture.

transfers.name: Release
transfers.comment: The flux out of the far end of the path. Its rate is the path itself, so there is nothing to set: the block works it out from its own cells.

transfers.name: Drawn_off
transfers.comment: The well is flushed: each year its water is replaced well_flow / well_volume times, so its inventory is a steady state rather than an accumulation.

expressions.name: Well_concentration
expressions.comment: What arrives per year, diluted into the volume the well draws. `Rock` is the release out of the far end of the path.

model.name: Lotka–Volterra predator and prey
model.description:
The predator–prey equations of Lotka and Volterra: prey x breed at rate α and are eaten at β·x·y; predators y breed by eating, at δ·x·y, and die at rate γ. Each population's growth is its compartment's dy/dt term, and each reads the other compartment. With α = 1.5, β = 1, γ = 3 and δ = 1, and both populations starting at 1, they cycle round the equilibrium (γ/δ, α/β) = (3, 1.5) every 3.32 years, the predators' peaks trailing the prey's by about half a year.

The cycles neither grow nor fade, because δx − γ·ln x + βy − α·ln y is conserved along every orbit. That is the Invariant expression, which stays within 1e-7 of 2 over the twenty years here. How far it drifts is a direct measure of a solver's error: at the tolerance set here (1e-8) dp45 holds it to 1.4e-7 in 461 steps, while the second-order ros23 needs 6541 steps and drifts by 7e-6. Loosen the tolerance to 1e-4 and the invariant wanders by a few parts in a thousand.

cases.name: a run that does not hold
